attribution_finding: Sealy majority pp.354–357 contains the horizontal-instrumentality, vertical distinction and unlawful price-fixing discussion; final 'which was illegal per se' is reporter syllabus p.350, not a continuation of the quoted opinion. Topco first sentence is majority at 608; second is a paraphrase presented as a quote.
fidelity_finding: Genuine fragments are stitched with altered connective wording; 'territorial exclusivity ... connection' drops 'But its' without brackets. The final relative clause transfers syllabus wording into opinion text. Topco's later formulation expands away its expressly horizontal context.
pinpoint_finding: Supplied 352–354,357–358 omits p.356 containing the essential price-fixing connection; use 354–357 and separately identify syllabus 350 if retained. Topco relevant text at 608, with further clarification at 609 n.9.
scope_and_cutoff_finding: Sealy's price-fixing-linked horizontal arrangements must not be broadened to every vertical license restraint. Topco (1972) is after the assigned 1970 cutoff; label later retrospective authority, exclude from as-of evidentiary support.
proposed_action_not_applied: Correct quotation boundaries and source labels; preserve and corroborate semantic_followup_02 rather than overwriting it.

ledger_excerpt:
From United States v. Sealy, Inc., 388 U.S. 350, 352–354, 357–358 (1967):
"Sealy, Inc., is an instrumentality of the licensees for purposes of the horizontal territorial allocation. It is not the principal. Accordingly, this case is to be distinguished from White Motor Co. v. United States... which involved a vertical territorial limitation... In the present case, we are also faced with an 'aggregation of trade restraints.'... territorial exclusivity... connection with the unlawful price-fixing is enough to require that it be condemned as an unlawful restraint... which was illegal per se."   
From United States v. Topco Associates, Inc., 405 U.S. 596, 608 (1972):
"One of the classic examples of a per se violation of § 1 is an agreement between competitors at the same level of the market structure to allocate territories in order to minimize competition... This Court has reiterated that an allocation of markets by agreement is a per se violation of the Sherman Act."
